choices.text: Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint and a forwarding rule to send queries for the default name to an internet DNS server to be resolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allow the entire VPC CIDR on port 443 in the inbound rules of the endpoint security group so that connections succeed even if the default name resolves to a public IP.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable the DNS hostnames attribute of the VPC, and then turn on enabling the private DNS name for the endpoint.

explanation: To use a private DNS name, both DNS resolution and the DNS hostnames attribute of the VPC must be turned on. Once hostnames is turned on, the endpoint resolves the default service name to the endpoint's private IP inside the VPC, so no code changes are needed. Changing to the endpoint-specific DNS name violates the constraint against code changes. An outbound endpoint and internet DNS forwarding would instead cause the name to resolve to a public IP. Allowing the security group does not change the name resolution problem.

prompt: An OU managed by AWS Control Tower already has 300 running Amazon RDS instances, and some of them have storage encryption turned off. The security team wants to view the list and status of the currently noncompliant databases on a dashboard without interrupting applications, and does not want to block existing operations or new deployments. Control Tower is already managing the accounts registered in the landing zone, and the security team wants to see the control status for each OU on a single screen. The RDS instances to be investigated number 300, spread across 40 accounts. The security team will carry out the encryption conversion separately after a schedule is set, so for now it needs only to understand the current state. The team wants to view noncompliance by OU on the Control Tower dashboard, and the development team is concerned that schedules will slip if new database deployments are interrupted. Which control type will meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A preventive control, which uses an SCP to deny at the organizational unit level the action of creating an unencrypted RDS instance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mandatory control, which applies to the OU the default controls that protect the resources deployed by Control Tower, to check RDS encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A detective control, in which an AWS Config rule evaluates the resources in the accounts and shows the noncompliant state as a violation on the dashboard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A proactive control, in which an AWS CloudFormation hook inspects the template before provisioning and stops the creation of noncompliant resources.

explanation: The correct answer is a detective control. A detective control is implemented with an AWS Config rule, evaluates existing resources in the accounts, shows states such as clear or in violation on the dashboard, and does not block operations. A preventive control denies actions with a policy such as an SCP, so it cannot report the state of existing resources and blocks later operations, which conflicts with the requirements. A proactive control only inspects resources provisioned through CloudFormation before they are created and does not evaluate databases that are already running. Mandatory controls protect the resources that Control Tower deployed and are unrelated to checking RDS encryption.

prompt: The key of an IAM user with administrator permissions in one member account of AWS Organizations has been leaked, and an attacker is creating resources. No one is responsible for the root user credentials of this account, so they cannot be used. The team wants to stop the attacker's activity immediately while preserving evidence without deleting resources, and to allow only one designated response role, IR-Forensics, to be used for the investigation. The attacker may have already created additional IAM users and roles, so the entire account must be controlled at once. The attacker has already created dozens of EC2 instances and S3 buckets, and the billing amount for the affected account continues to grow. The legal team requires that the state of the resources be preserved as is. Access must be blocked before checking the IAM users or roles the attacker created, and the organization's management account continues to be responsible for the billing information of this account. Which action is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From the management account, attach to the account an SCP that denies all actions except for the response role.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a script that sets permissions boundaries on all IAM users and roles to reduce the scope of permissions the attacker can use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Remove the account from the organization to make it a standalone account, register billing information separately, and completely isolate it from the other accounts in the organization.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Close the account to put it in a suspended state, and then investigate the resources of the closed account within the suspension period to secure evidence.

explanation: The correct answer is to attach to the account an SCP that denies everything except the response role. An SCP restricts the requests of all IAM users and roles in the member account, including the root user, so an attacker with administrator permissions is blocked, the resources remain as they are, and only the role allowed by the condition can investigate. Removing the account from the organization loses the SCP control from above and leaves no means of stopping the attacker. Closing the account puts it in a suspended state, which makes investigative access difficult, and the content is deleted after the suspension period. A permissions boundary can be removed or bypassed by an attacker with administrator permissions.

prompt: A security audit has requested a list of software vulnerabilities for all instances. The account has 300 EC2 Linux instances, 40 of which do not have the SSM Agent, and security policy does not allow installing an agent. The 40 instances are EBS-backed with an ext4 file system and 2 volumes totaling 500 GB. The remaining 260 instances are already managed with the SSM Agent, Amazon Inspector is not enabled, and the audit deadline is 2 weeks away. The 40 instances are in production, so they must be assessed without restarting or installing software, and the results must be delivered as a CVE list for each instance. The account uses Inspector only in the Seoul Region. Which method requires the fewest changes to obtain OS package vulnerability results for these instances without installing an agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep the Amazon Inspector scan mode agent-based, and deploy the SSM Agent and an instance profile in bulk to the 40 instances to convert them into managed instances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the Amazon Inspector EC2 scan mode to hybrid scanning so that instances not managed by SSM receive agentless scanning based on EBS snapshots.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 to periodically scan the volumes of the 40 instances and receive the OS package vulnerability list as the result.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on Amazon Inspector ECR container image scanning and judge host vulnerabilities instead from the vulnerabilities of the images deployed on the instances.

explanation: Inspector's hybrid scan mode applies agent-based scanning to instances managed by SSM and agentless scanning that reads EBS snapshots to unmanaged instances, and these instances meet the conditions of being EBS-backed, using ext4, having fewer than 8 volumes, and totaling 1,200 GB or less. Keeping agent-based scanning conflicts with the constraint that an agent cannot be installed. Malware Protection for EC2 is malware detection and not package vulnerability scanning. ECR image scanning cannot substitute for the host OS packages.

prompt: About 50,000 files are uploaded per day, with varied extensions and sizes. There is one Amazon S3 bucket (ap-northeast-2) to which customers upload documents, and this account does not use GuardDuty. The security team wants to scan only the uploaded files for malware without turning on all of GuardDuty, and it needs to receive the scan results as object tags or events and automatically decide whether to quarantine. Most uploaded objects are a few MB in size, and some PDF and Office documents reach hundreds of MB. The quarantine handling has already been built with AWS Lambda, and it is acceptable for the scan charges to be proportional to the upload volume. The bucket policy uses presigned URLs for uploads from outside, and the upload path cannot be changed. Objects determined to be quarantine targets must be blocked from access immediately. Which configuration meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on GuardDuty Malware Protection for S3 as a standalone feature for the bucket, and build the quarantine flow with scan result tagging or Amazon EventBridge events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on GuardDuty and S3 Protection in the account, treat anomaly detection findings based on AWS CloudTrail S3 data events as a malicious file verdict, and integrate a Lambda function that moves the object to a quarantine bucket when a finding appears.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run an Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery job every day to find malware signatures in the uploaded objects, and send the results to Amazon EventBridge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable Amazon Inspector and configure it to perform a vulnerability scan on every object uploaded to the bucket to determine whether the file is malicious.

explanation: Malware Protection for S3 can be turned on for a bucket as a standalone feature without enabling the GuardDuty service. It automatically scans newly uploaded objects and new versions, then publishes the results to EventBridge and a CloudWatch namespace, and tagging is also optional. The combination of all of GuardDuty and S3 Protection only detects anomalous behavior in S3 data events, does not scan file contents for malware, and is broader than the requested scope. Macie is a service for finding sensitive data and not a malware scanner. Inspector scans software vulnerabilities in EC2, ECR, and Lambda, so it does not fit determining whether an S3 object is malware.

prompt: A deployment pipeline runs on GitHub-hosted runners, and security policy prohibits storing long-term AWS keys in repository secrets. The company wants a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy to an AWS account without long-term access keys. Only workflows on the main branch of a specific repository, acme/web, must be able to assume the deployment role. The workflow runs in a single repository, acme/web, and the deployment target is a single account, and the security team wants to prevent workflows from other repositories or workflows on development branches from assuming this role. The deployment tool is the AWS CDK, and only one role will exist in the deployment account. The default value for the temporary credential lifetime is sufficient. Which TWO configurations are MOST appropriate to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Register the GitHub OIDC issuer token.actions.githubusercontent.com as an IAM OIDC identity provider.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the deployment role trust policy, allow sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity and set conditions with aud as sts.amazonaws.com and sub as repo:acme/web:ref:refs/heads/main.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the root of the AWS account owned by GitHub as the principal in the deployment role trust policy and allow sts:AssumeRole, to allow all GitHub workflows to assume the role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Store the access key of a deployment IAM user in the GitHub repository secrets, and operate a procedure in which a responsible person rotates the key every 90 days.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Put the entire IP range of GitHub-hosted runners in an aws:SourceIp condition on the deployment role and allow all requests coming from those IPs.

explanation: GitHub Actions authenticates to AWS with an OIDC token, so you register the issuer as an IAM OIDC provider, allow AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity in the role trust policy, and restrict the repository and branch with the aud and sub conditions. This way no long-term keys are needed. Access keys in repository secrets violate the requirement against long-term credentials, and rotation is manual. Trusting the GitHub account root would make any workflow or repository a possible caller. Allowing the runner IP ranges also allows the runners of other repositories.

prompt: A data protection team wants to centrally enforce that the S3 buckets and KMS keys in all member accounts of the organization do not allow access to principals from AWS accounts outside the organization. The control must block mistakes even if a development team adds a statement allowing an external account to a bucket policy, and because there are 150 accounts, modifying bucket policies one by one would be too heavy an operational burden. The team determined that, because the teams that own buckets differ from account to account, owner education alone cannot fully prevent such mistakes. There are no buckets legitimately shared with accounts outside the organization, and when external auditors need access, a separate account is invited into the organization for their use. Requests in which AWS services access buckets and keys on behalf of users must continue to work. The compliance team wants to apply this control to the entire organization at once and to manage change history with a single policy. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on the S3 account-level Block Public Access setting in all member accounts to block the path by which principals from external accounts access buckets and objects.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach to the organization root an RCP that uses the aws:PrincipalOrgID condition to deny S3 and KMS access by principals outside the organization, excluding requests from AWS service principals where aws:PrincipalIsAWSService is true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attach to the organization root a service control policy (SCP) that contains the same deny condition and the AWS service principal exception, to block S3 and KMS access by external principals all at once.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy, with AWS CloudFormation StackSets, bucket policies that contain a statement denying principals outside the organization to each bucket, and handle new buckets in the deployment pipeline.

explanation: The correct answer is to attach an RCP to the organization root. Placing an aws:PrincipalIsAWSService exception in the deny condition keeps requests that AWS service principals make on behalf of users allowed. An RCP sets the maximum permissions on resources in member accounts, and even if a resource-based policy allows an external account, it can block requests from principals outside the organization, and it supports S3 and KMS. An SCP restricts only IAM users and roles inside the organization and does not apply to requests from principals in external accounts. Block Public Access blocks public access but does not block access that is allowed to a specific external account principal. Deploying bucket policies with StackSets can be overwritten by bucket owners who can modify the policies, and KMS keys would need to be handled separately.

prompt: A financial company wants to continuously understand where personal information is located across thousands of S3 buckets in its organization's 120 accounts while minimizing cost, and to run a precise full-object scan on only a few buckets that appear to be high risk. The personal information to be identified includes common types such as credit card numbers and bank account numbers, and the 4 members of the security team will review the results every month. Some buckets have been reported in the past as having public read status. New buckets are continually created, the total data volume is several PB, and there are no staff to build and operate separate analysis code. Most buckets are archives with few changes, and a precise scan is needed only for the buckets that the security team designates. The results must be viewable for the entire organization in one place. The number of accounts and buckets keeps growing, so new buckets must also automatically become evaluation targets. Which approach is MOST cost-effective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an AWS Lambda function for each bucket to read objects and analyze personal information with Amazon Comprehend, and store the results in a central bucket.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on GuardDuty S3 Protection across the organization and configure it to detect the personal information types contained in objects along with anomalous access.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turn on automated sensitive data discovery across the organization, and run discovery jobs only on the buckets with high sensitivity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a sensitive data discovery job that targets all buckets and repeats daily, so that all objects are analyzed without omission every day.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination of automated sensitive data discovery and targeted discovery jobs. Automated discovery continuously evaluates the bucket inventory, selects representative objects as samples to analyze, and provides broad visibility through sensitivity scores and heatmaps at a low cost, while jobs analyze risky buckets in greater depth. Running a daily job on all buckets repeatedly analyzes all objects, which makes the cost large. A per-bucket Lambda function with Comprehend requires direct implementation and management. GuardDuty S3 Protection detects anomalous access and does not identify personal information inside objects.

prompt: An e-commerce company's security team is strengthening its data loss prevention policy and wants to apply the same rule to both development and production accounts. Under the organization's policy, instances in a VPC must not be able to copy data through an S3 gateway endpoint to buckets in external AWS accounts that are not owned by the organization. Recently, a developer uploaded test data to a bucket in a personal account. The organization has many accounts, the company's own policies cannot be applied to external buckets, and access to buckets inside the organization must remain as it is now. Endpoints have already been created for each VPC, and there is no case in which data needs to be exchanged with external partners. The policy must be applied in the same way to new VPCs as well. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deploy bucket policies that deny external account principals to all S3 buckets in the organization, to block copy requests to other accounts from the bucket side.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remove the S3 prefix list from the outbound rules of the instance security groups, and allow access to organization buckets only through the NAT gateway path.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the S3 gateway endpoint policy, allow S3 actions only on resources where aws:ResourceOrgID equals the organization ID.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a rule to the VPC subnet NACL that denies the domain name of buckets in external accounts, to block data copy requests before they leave.

explanation: The endpoint policy applies to requests going from the VPC to S3, and allowing only when the target resource is owned by the organization, by using the aws:ResourceOrgID condition, blocks copying to buckets in external accounts while keeping access to organization buckets. A bucket policy applies only to the organization's own buckets, so it cannot control requests that write to external buckets. Removing the prefix list and using a NAT path instead leaves an internet path for reaching external buckets. A NACL works on IP and port and cannot deny bucket domain names.

prompt: A broker service in a multi-tenant SaaS creates a new session for each request, calls AssumeRole on the per-tenant role tenant-role, and passes a session policy along with it. The role's identity-based policy allows only s3:GetObject on the entire bucket. The session policy passed with each call allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on the tenantA/ prefix. The development team is verifying whether this configuration isolates tenants from each other and whether writes also work. The bucket policy has no separate denies or allows, and the session was created for tenantA. The broker runs in one of the organization's accounts, and the team wants to check only the policy configuration without code changes. Which is the MOST accurate description of the results of the actions that the tenantA session attempts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both reading and writing objects under tenantA/ succeed, and only reading objects under tenantB/ is denied because it is outside the scope of the session policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only reading objects under tenantA/ succeeds, and both writing objects under tenantA/ and reading objects under tenantB/ are denied.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading and writing objects under tenantA/ succeed, and reading objects under tenantB/ also succeeds because the role policy allows it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the session policy takes precedence over the role policy, all actions succeed, including writes to the tenantA/ prefix that the session policy allows.

explanation: A session policy does not grant permissions and only reduces the permissions allowed by the role's identity-based policy, and the effective permissions of the session are the intersection of the two policies. Reading is allowed by both policies, so reading tenantA/ objects succeeds. Writing is not allowed by the role policy, so it is denied even though the session policy allows it. Reading tenantB/ is allowed by the role policy but is not in the session policy, so it is denied. Any explanation that the session policy increases permissions beyond the role policy is wrong.

prompt: The security team of a company that creates 5 to 10 new accounts per month aims for consistent policy application without manual checks. The team created an AWS Firewall Manager AWS WAF policy so that an AWS WAF web ACL is automatically associated with all ALBs, including those in new accounts, across the 40 accounts of an AWS Organizations organization. However, in some accounts the resources within the policy scope are not evaluated and the noncompliant state persists. The policy itself and the organization configuration have been confirmed to be correct, and the Firewall Manager administrator account is also designated. Most of the problem accounts recently joined the organization. The administrator checked the status of those accounts in the Firewall Manager console, and they are not accounts excluded from the policy scope. Several weeks have passed since the policy was created. What should be checked and fixed first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an inbound allow rule to the ALB security group of those accounts so that the Firewall Manager service can access it, to allow the policy association.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the policy scope to the management account alone, move the ALBs to the management account, and have the same policy evaluated within a single account.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Issue an IAM user access key in each account, and configure the Firewall Manager administrator account to associate web ACLs with those keys.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Verify that AWS Config is enabled and recording resource configurations in the accounts and Regions included in the policy scope, and turn it on where it is off.

explanation: Firewall Manager can evaluate resources and apply rules only when AWS Config is enabled in the accounts and Regions within the policy scope, and accounts in which Config is off remain noncompliant or unevaluated. The service works through service-linked roles and the Organizations integration rather than security group rules, so allowing it in a security group is irrelevant. Moving ALBs to the management account gives up the goal of automatic protection across the whole organization. Issuing access keys increases long-term credentials and is not how Firewall Manager works.

prompt: A role in account B must read S3 objects that are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key in account A. The two accounts are in different OUs of the same organization, and the objects are encrypted with SSE-KMS. The IAM policy of the account B role has an allow for kms:Decrypt on the key ARN, and the access allow on the S3 bucket side is also in place, but decryption fails with AccessDenied. The key policy in account A has only the default statement for the account A root. The key is also used by other workloads in account A, so account A's existing access method must not be changed. Account B is operated by another team, the security administrator of account A can modify the key policy directly, and the deployment deadline is within this week. Which resolution is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the account B IAM policy allow already exists, have the account A root user delete the default statement of the key policy so that only account B uses the key.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In account A, convert the key to a multi-Region key to create a replica, and change the key ID so that account B decrypts with the replica.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the account A key ARN explicitly with a Condition in the kms:Decrypt allow of the account B role policy, to make the cross-account allow scope more specific.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add to the account A key policy a statement that allows kms:Decrypt with the account B account or that role as the principal.

explanation: KMS key access is based on the key policy. For a principal in another account to use the key, the key policy must allow that account or principal, and the calling account's IAM policy must also allow it. The key policy has only account A, so account B's request is denied. Deleting the default statement also removes the delegation to IAM policies in account A itself, which actually makes access management harder. Multi-Region keys are for replication across Regions and cannot replace a cross-account access allow. Adding a condition to the IAM policy does not resolve the absence of an allow in the key policy.

prompt: A public subnet that hosts a public web service accepts connections from the internet on TCP 443. Currently, the NACL for this subnet has, besides the default deny rule, only one rule, numbered 100, that allows inbound TCP 443 from all IPs. This morning, attack traffic was confirmed to be coming from 198.51.100.0/24. Normal user access to the service must continue to be allowed, and without touching the security groups, only this range must be blocked at the subnet boundary within minutes. The subnet has 12 web servers, and the service spans multiple Availability Zones. NACLs are managed per subnet, and the current change history is retained in AWS CloudTrail. The blocking rule must be easy to remove after the attack stops. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add an inbound deny rule for 198.51.100.0/24 TCP 443 to the NACL as rule number 200, so that the range is blocked after the existing allow rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add an inbound deny rule for 198.51.100.0/24 TCP 443 to the NACL with a number lower than 100, so that it is evaluated before the allow rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Add a deny entry for 198.51.100.0/24 to the inbound rules of the web server security group to block HTTPS requests from that range in front of the servers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a route for the destination 198.51.100.0/24 to the subnet route table so that response traffic is directed to a blackhole target, cutting off the connections.

explanation: NACL rules are evaluated starting from the lowest number, and the first matching rule is applied, so the deny rule must be given a number lower than the allow rule 100 so that the range is blocked before it reaches the allow rule. A deny rule numbered 200 is never evaluated because rule 100 matches first. Security groups have only allow rules and cannot have deny rules. Changing the response route cannot prevent the TCP connection from being established, so it is unreliable, and it also fails to meet the requirement to block at the subnet boundary.

prompt: A company wants users of its mobile app to sign up with email and, after signing in, have the app upload directly only to their own S3 prefix, uploads/{unique user ID}/. There are an average of 200,000 users per day, and uploads are made directly from the app, so they must be handled without server involvement. The development team has 3 members and has no capacity to create per-user policies separately or to operate an upload server. The app must obtain temporary AWS credentials without going through a server, and the company wants to handle per-user prefix isolation with a single policy. User information is stored in an Amazon Cognito user pool at email sign-up, and uploaded objects need to be read and written only by the user. The mobile app already uses the AWS SDK. Latency only needs to be at a level that does not affect the start of an upload. Which configuration is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Have the app present the ID token issued by the Cognito user pool directly to Amazon S3 for authentication, restrict the prefix in the bucket policy by the sub claim of the token, and when the token expires, have the app obtain a new token from the user pool with a refresh token and present it again.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Build an Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda upload proxy so that the app sends the file to Lambda, and Lambda adds the prefix by user ID and stores it in Amazon S3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sign in with the Cognito user pool, obtain temporary credentials for the authenticated role through an identity pool, and restrict the prefix in the role policy by using the cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub policy variable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Issue an IAM user and access key for each user and store it in the app, and attach an individual IAM policy that uses the user name as the prefix.

explanation: The user pool handles authentication and token issuance, and the identity pool issues temporary credentials for an IAM role to authenticated users. Using the cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub policy variable in the role policy isolates per-user prefixes with a single policy. S3 does not directly authenticate user pool JWTs. A Lambda proxy creates problems with the requirement not to go through a server and with the cost of relaying upload data. Per-user IAM users and long-term keys are inappropriate for both security and management.

prompt: After a breach, an auditor requires proof that the CloudTrail log files accumulated in the central S3 bucket over the last 90 days were not modified or deleted after delivery. The trail had log file integrity validation turned on from the beginning, and there are records of an attacker with administrator permissions attempting to access this bucket. The bucket is in the security account, and the logs contain management events from all Regions, with a retention period of 1 year. While the attacker was attempting access, objects in the log delivery bucket may have been deleted, so the auditor wants signature-based evidence. The validation will be performed in the security account, and the logs are stored in the bucket with SSE-S3. The security team wants to provide the proof using the method that CloudTrail provides by default, without building new tools or a separate server. Which method is MOST appropriate to meet this requirement with no additional infrastructure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use the CLI validate-logs command to verify the digest file signatures and the log file hashes for that period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply S3 Object Lock in compliance mode to the bucket now, and explain to the auditor that the logs from the past 90 days could not have been modified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Query the bucket configuration change history in the AWS Config timeline, and present it as evidence that the contents of the log objects did not change.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Import the CloudTrail event history into a new event data store, and report by comparing whether the event count equals the count in the original logs.

explanation: The correct answer is to verify the digest files with validate-logs. When integrity validation is turned on, CloudTrail creates a hash for each log file and delivers a signed digest file to the same bucket every hour, so you can use SHA-256 and RSA signatures to check whether a file was modified or deleted after delivery. Because the feature was already turned on, there is no retroactivity problem. Object Lock only prevents future deletions and cannot prove that past data was not tampered with. The configuration history in AWS Config cannot show changes to object contents. Comparing counts cannot cryptographically prove that the contents were not tampered with.

prompt: Amazon GuardDuty reported a finding about an unusual API call pattern from an IAM role in a development account. The analyst does not want to use SQL and wants to follow the IP addresses, other accounts, and resources associated with this role and compare them with normal activity to judge the scope of the damage. The period under investigation is the last 3 months, and the analyst is not given separate access to the raw log storage. The analyst must report the investigation results within one day, and the account is linked to other accounts in the organization through IAM role chaining, so the analyst must also check whether the damage spread to other accounts. The role under investigation is used jointly by the CI pipeline and developers in the development account and has high activity volume. Which service meets this requirement while minimizing the work of collecting and parsing logs directly?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a CloudTrail log table with Amazon Athena and directly query the call history per role ARN to narrow down the anomaly times and counterpart resources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use Amazon Detective to move from the finding to the role's entity profile and review the activity of the connected IPs and resources through the behavior graph.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scan the software vulnerabilities of the instances that use the role with Amazon Inspector, and trace back the breach path and affected resources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aggregate the findings across accounts and Regions with AWS Security Hub, then create a custom insight to examine the role's call trend and connected targets.

explanation: The correct answer is Amazon Detective. Detective builds a behavior graph from logs such as CloudTrail and VPC flow logs and lets you move directly from a GuardDuty finding to an entity profile and visualize the relationships among IPs, accounts, and resources, which suits the scoping stage. Security Hub aggregates and organizes findings but does not provide a log-based behavior graph or entity activity comparison. Athena requires you to write SQL and prepare tables yourself, which conflicts with the no-SQL condition and with minimizing operational burden. Inspector is a vulnerability scanner, so its purpose differs from investigating the scope of damage from API call patterns.

prompt: It has been confirmed that a developer committed the access key of the IAM user deploy-bot to a public GitHub repository. This key may also be used in one nightly deployment pipeline, so the company must be able to check whether a usage site is interrupted and, if necessary, roll back. At the same time, use by an attacker must be blocked right now. Key usage history can be queried through CloudTrail, but the developer who created the key has left for the day and cannot be reached. The commit history of the public repository includes the secret value of the key, and this user has broad write permissions. The pipeline is scheduled to run once within 2 hours after the leak notice. The IAM user has no other access keys and does not use console access, and the security team plans to schedule the key rotation after the investigation. Which first action is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detach all policies attached to the user, delete the user, and create a new user with the same name to clean up the impact of the key leak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Change the access key to the inactive state and check the call records for the key ID in CloudTrail.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delete the access key immediately, issue a new key and deploy it to the pipeline configuration, and check the usage history of the old key in CloudTrail.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reset the IAM user's console password and register a new MFA device so that the attacker can no longer use the user account.

explanation: The correct answer is to change the key to the inactive state. Deactivation blocks authentication immediately while allowing the key to be reactivated, so it fits the requirement to check whether the pipeline actually uses this key and then restore it, and searching CloudTrail by key ID also lets you trace the attacker's activity. Deleting the key cannot be undone, so there is no way to roll back if the pipeline stops. The console password and MFA affect only console sign-in and have no effect on access key authentication. Deleting and re-creating the user is excessive, cannot be undone, and loses the linkage information needed for the investigation.

prompt: A company has AWS Network Firewall in an inspection VPC (10.100.0.0/16) and centrally inspects the outbound traffic of spoke VPCs (10.1.0.0/16, 10.2.0.0/16) through AWS Transit Gateway. The company put only .example.com in the domain list allow rule group, but HTTPS leaving the spoke VPCs passes even for domains that are not on the list. The firewall policy is already associated with the Transit Gateway attachment path, and the domain list in the stateful rule group is evaluated based on the HTTP host header and the TLS SNI. No variables were set separately for the domain list rule group, so it remains at the default values. The operations team has 2 members and wants to avoid additional configuration such as certificate deployment. Traffic is several TB per day, and increases in latency must be minimized. Firewall endpoints are already deployed in each Availability Zone. What should be done to apply domain filtering with the fewest changes and without TLS decryption?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Modify the HOME_NET variable of the rule group to include the CIDR ranges of the inspection VPC and both spoke VPCs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a TLS inspection configuration to the firewall policy and decrypt all HTTPS sessions with an ACM certificate to filter based on the body instead of the SNI.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch the firewall policy rule evaluation order to strict order, and change the stateless default action so that traffic is not forwarded to the stateful engine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy a separate Network Firewall and domain rule group for each spoke VPC so that each VPC uses its own CIDR as the home network.

explanation: Domain list inspection by default filters only traffic within the range of HOME_NET, which is the CIDR of the VPC where the firewall is deployed, so to inspect traffic from other VPCs coming through Transit Gateway, you must manually add those CIDRs to HOME_NET. HTTPS domains are determined by SNI, so TLS decryption is not needed. Changing the evaluation order or the stateless default action does not change the reason that traffic outside HOME_NET does not match the domain rules. Deploying a firewall per VPC abandons the centralized inspection architecture, and the changes and cost are large.

prompt: A company issued a *.example.com public certificate with ACM in the Seoul Region and completed DNS validation. However, this certificate does not appear in the custom SSL certificate list of the CloudFront distribution. The domain's DNS is managed in Route 53, and no person should have to track the certificate renewal schedule separately. The domain is also used by an ALB in the Seoul Region, so the Seoul certificate is still needed for the ALB. The CloudFront distribution already exists, and the domain name is registered as an alternate domain name (CNAME). The CNAME record for DNS validation has already been created in Route 53, and certificate issuance takes only a few minutes. The company wants to make changes only in the distribution settings on the CloudFront side. How can the problem be resolved with the fewest changes while keeping the certificate in an automatically renewing state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Re-create the distribution in the Seoul Region so that the CloudFront distribution can use the Seoul Region certificate, and also move the origin server settings to be Seoul-based.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turn on cross-Region replication of the Seoul certificate in the ACM settings so that a copy of the same certificate is automatically created in the Region that CloudFront uses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manually upload the Seoul Region certificate to the IAM certificate store as if it were an external CA certificate, attach it to the CloudFront distribution, and renew it yourself before it expires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Newly issue an ACM public certificate for the same domain with DNS validation in the US East (N. Virginia) Region, and attach it to the CloudFront distribution.

explanation: The correct answer is to newly issue an ACM certificate in US East (N. Virginia) (us-east-1). ACM certificates are Regional resources and CloudFront uses only ACM certificates in us-east-1, so if you issue one in that Region and keep DNS validation, ACM renews it automatically. Uploading to the IAM certificate store is manual management and violates the automatic renewal requirement. CloudFront is a global service, so a distribution cannot be moved to the Seoul Region. ACM has no feature to automatically replicate a certificate between Regions.

prompt: The security team received a report that abnormally long domain queries are going out from 200 servers in the Seoul Region and suspects DNS tunneling. The instances run in a VPC that uses the default Amazon DNS, and the security team had turned on VPC flow logs, but no queried domain names were found, and even the traffic going to the Amazon DNS server did not appear in the records. The servers are in production, so restarting them or installing an agent is difficult, and the security team has 3 members and has no capacity to operate a new separate analysis system. All the servers are in private subnets of the same VPC, and the team wants to retain query records for 90 days for use in forensics. The only DNS currently used is the VPC default resolver, and there are no custom DNS servers. What should be done with the fewest changes to obtain the queried domain names?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Customize the VPC flow log record format to add a query domain field, and reduce the maximum aggregation interval to 1 minute to collect again.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a Traffic Mirroring session on every instance network interface and configure a fleet of separate analysis appliances to interpret the DNS packets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Modify the trail to enable the Route 53 item of CloudTrail data events so that DNS queries sent by instances are recorded as API calls.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure Route 53 Resolver query logging for that VPC, associate the VPC, and deliver the query logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3.

explanation: Traffic to and from the default Amazon DNS server is not recorded in VPC flow logs, and flow logs have no domain name field either, so the queried names are obtained by associating Route 53 Resolver query logging with the VPC. Customizing the format cannot add a domain field that does not exist and does not change what is collected. Traffic Mirroring and analysis appliances impose a very large configuration and operational burden compared with the requirement. DNS queries from instances are not recorded as CloudTrail events.

prompt: The 40 accounts in a sandbox OU must be able to use only four services: Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon CloudWatch, and any new services that AWS releases in the future must be automatically blocked until the SCP is explicitly modified. Currently, the default FullAWSAccess SCP is attached to this OU, and other OUs must be left unchanged. When a new account moves into this OU, the same restriction must be applied automatically without extra work. The sandbox OU is for developer experimentation and uses only the Seoul Region. The security team wants SCP changes to be made only through an approval process, and the core goal is to prevent new services from being used unnoticed. Which configuration is MOST appropriate to meet the requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detach FullAWSAccess from the organization root and attach an SCP that allows only the four services to the root, to restrict the allowed scope for the entire organization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detach FullAWSAccess from the sandbox OU and attach an SCP that allows only the four services. Leave the root as it is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Keep FullAWSAccess and additionally attach to the sandbox OU an SCP that allows the four services, to restrict the allowed scope to the four services.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep FullAWSAccess and attach to the sandbox OU an SCP that denies all currently known services except the four, to restrict them.

explanation: The correct answer is to replace FullAWSAccess on the sandbox OU. For a permission to be allowed, there must be an explicit Allow at every level from the root to the account, so keeping a full allow at the root and having only an SCP that allows the four services on the sandbox OU turns that OU into an allow list alone, and new services are denied by default. If FullAWSAccess remains at the same level, the allows are merged and effectively everything is allowed. A method that denies known services automatically allows services released later. Replacing it at the root would restrict other OUs as well, which violates the requirement.

prompt: Five teams, including the analytics, marketing, and finance teams, share a single data lake bucket. Each team has different prefixes it can access, and the analytics team's access must be allowed only from within a specific VPC. The bucket policy has grown to hundreds of lines, and incidents in which changing one place affects other teams keep recurring. The data is separated by prefix, and multiple pipelines depend on this bucket, so splitting or migrating the bucket itself is difficult given the schedule. Per-team access history is reported separately in audits, and the work of migrating each team's application to use a new access path can be scheduled team by team. Which method separates per-team permission management with the LEAST risk without splitting the bucket?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Keep adding only per-team IAM policies, and put an allow for all prefixes in a single statement in the bucket policy so that no policy edits are needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a separate bucket for each team and use S3 replication to copy the data lake prefixes to each team's bucket, to completely separate access permissions by team.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an S3 access point and a per-prefix policy for each team, and make the analytics team's access point accept only requests from the designated VPC.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put all the aws:SourceVpce conditions and per-prefix conditions in a single bucket policy, to manage allow rules by team and network path in one policy.

explanation: The correct answer is a per-team S3 access point. Each access point applies its own policy and network controls and can be configured to accept only requests coming from a VPC, and access point policies are evaluated together with the bucket policy, so team rules are separated and a change in one place does not spread to other teams. Only adding IAM policies and allowing all prefixes in the bucket policy loses per-prefix separation and the VPC restriction. Creating a bucket for each team and replicating violates the constraint of not splitting the bucket. Putting all conditions in a single policy leaves the current problem as it is.

prompt: A company that operates dozens of payment-related microservices runs an Amazon EKS cluster built with EC2 node groups (not Fargate). The security team wants to use Amazon GuardDuty to detect both runtime behavior, such as malicious processes and file access running inside containers, and anonymous access and privilege escalation attempts against the Kubernetes API server. GuardDuty is already enabled in the account, and the team does not want to manage EKS control plane logging itself. The nodes are based on Amazon Linux, and the team wants to avoid introducing a new separate security product. The cluster is a single cluster in the Seoul Region, and the namespace to be monitored is a single production environment. The security team wants to merge the results directly into the existing GuardDuty findings flow. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate to meet these two requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on Amazon Inspector ECR scanning to detect malicious processes in running containers in real time and deliver the results to the security team.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring and deploy the GuardDuty security agent to the cluster to collect OS-level events from containers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the cluster VPC to publish flow logs to Amazon S3 so that GuardDuty can analyze the network activity of containers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable GuardDuty EKS Audit Log Monitoring to analyze suspicious activity targeting the API server from the Kubernetes audit logs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enable GuardDuty Lambda Protection to analyze process execution and file access events of containers in the cluster nodes.

explanation: Audit Log Monitoring analyzes activity targeting the API server, such as anonymous access and privilege escalation, from Kubernetes audit logs, and Runtime Monitoring detects malicious behavior by having a security agent collect process, file, and network events from containers. Each of the two features handles one requirement. Lambda Protection targets the network activity of Lambda functions, so it is unrelated to EKS nodes. Inspector ECR scanning is image vulnerability scanning and not detection of running processes. GuardDuty analyzes flow logs through its own independent stream, so the user does not need to publish flow logs.

prompt: A company connects a central inspection VPC, with firewall endpoints in two Availability Zones, to a transit gateway to inspect traffic between spoke VPCs. The firewall endpoints are healthy in both zones and there are no errors in the route tables. However, TCP communication between spoke VPCs in different Availability Zones is intermittently dropped, and logs show that the stateful firewall's session state does not match. Communication within the same Availability Zone is normal. The service is in production, and for availability reasons the workloads cannot be consolidated into one zone, and the change must be completed on the inspection VPC side. The failure appears only for some flows at the moment a new connection is created, and monitoring has not shown a shortage of throughput. What should be done to resolve this problem with the fewest changes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's transit gateway VPC attachment so that the round trip of a flow passes through the appliance in the same Availability Zone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add two firewall endpoints in each Availability Zone and adjust the transit gateway route table to an evenly distributed path to increase throughput.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the firewall policy's stateless default action to drop so that all packets whose state does not match are discarded and the client retransmits them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Merge the spoke VPC subnets by Availability Zone and move all workloads to one Availability Zone to eliminate cross-Availability Zone traffic altogether.

explanation: When appliance mode is turned on, the transit gateway selects one network interface in the inspection VPC by hashing for each flow and uses the same interface for the round-trip traffic until the flow ends. Symmetric routing to the same Availability Zone is therefore guaranteed, and stateful inspection keeps session state consistently. Adding endpoints does not resolve the asymmetry in which the round trip splits across different Availability Zones. Changing the stateless default action to drop can discard normal traffic as well. Consolidating workloads into one Availability Zone undermines the availability requirement.

prompt: A company collects GuardDuty findings from 60 accounts in AWS Organizations into a delegated administrator account. When a finding of the InstanceCredentialExfiltration type occurs, indicating that EC2 instance role credentials were used from an external IP, the sessions of that role must be automatically invalidated within 5 minutes. The company wants to avoid the operational burden of building separate detection infrastructure for each account. From detection to remediation, the process must complete automatically with no human judgment, and a dedicated response IAM role is already deployed in the target accounts. The audit team must be able to look up the response records later. The role subject to session revocation is used as an instance profile, and deleting or re-creating the role is not allowed. In case of a false positive, the affected workload must recover immediately with a new session. Which automated response configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaluate IAM role configurations with an AWS Config organization rule, and attach a remediation action so that Systems Manager Automation revokes sessions when a noncompliant role is found.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create CloudTrail metric filters and Amazon CloudWatch alarms in every account, notify the responsible person through Amazon SNS, and have the responsible person revoke the role sessions directly in the console.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have an Amazon EventBridge rule in the delegated administrator account match the finding and invoke AWS Lambda, and have Lambda attach the session revocation policy through the response role in the target account.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Export GuardDuty findings to Amazon S3 in each account, run an Amazon Athena query every hour, and have AWS Lambda revoke sessions when that type is found.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination of an EventBridge rule and Lambda in the delegated administrator account. GuardDuty sends findings to EventBridge in near real time, and a rule in the delegated administrator account also reacts to findings from member accounts, so a single rule automatically handles 60 accounts and meets the 5-minute requirement. Per-account metric filters and alarms must be configured in each account and involve humans, which fits neither the speed nor the operational burden requirements. A Config rule only evaluates configuration state and does not take GuardDuty findings or anomalous credential usage as input. Exporting to S3 and hourly Athena queries cannot meet the 5-minute target.

prompt: A media company's KMS request costs have surged because of billions of GET requests per month on an S3 bucket encrypted with SSE-KMS using a customer managed key. The client code cannot be changed, and the use of the customer managed key and the CloudTrail audit requirement must be maintained. Even after S3 Bucket Keys were turned on for the bucket, KMS calls did not decrease when existing objects were read. The data consists of about 800 million objects, and most objects are read several times a day. Objects are mostly small and are not modified, and bulk copy jobs can be run during the weekend maintenance window. There are 800 million objects, mostly small files, and read service must continue while the existing objects are copied. Cost analysis shows that the number of KMS requests is the main cause of the charges. Which additional action reduces the cost MOST efficiently?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an S3 Batch Operations copy objects job to copy the existing objects in place so that they are re-encrypted with the Bucket Key applied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Switch the bucket default encryption to dual-layer server-side encryption (DSSE-KMS) so that the number of KMS requests is reduced together with Bucket Keys.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Switch the bucket default encryption to SSE-S3 so that no KMS requests occur, and substitute S3 server access logs for object access auditing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on automatic rotation of the KMS customer managed key so that the key material changes periodically and the KMS request cost on object reads decreases.

explanation: The correct answer is to copy the existing objects so that Bucket Keys are applied. A Bucket Key applies only to objects written after it is configured, and existing objects do not use a Bucket Key. Rewriting them with CopyObject applies it, so the objects can be copied in bulk with a Batch Operations job. Switching to SSE-S3 violates the customer managed key and KMS-based audit requirements. DSSE-KMS does not support Bucket Keys. Automatic key rotation only changes the key material and has nothing to do with the number or cost of KMS requests generated by reading objects.

prompt: An SCP allow list approach has been applied to all member accounts in the development OU. In this OU, the default FullAWSAccess SCP was detached, and the SCP attached to the OU allows only ec2:* and s3:*. FullAWSAccess remains at the organization root. In one member account in this OU, a developer's IAM user has the AdministratorAccess managed policy attached directly, and the developer has asked since yesterday why they cannot create RDS instances. The security team wants to explain the cause with the policy evaluation logic. The user has no permissions boundary and no session policy is used. The SCP at the organization root is not being changed, and the account in question was recently moved to that OU. Which is the MOST accurate description of this user's effective permissions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The user can perform EC2 and S3 actions, but creating RDS instances, which the SCP does not allow, is denied even with the administrator policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the administrator policy allows all actions, all service actions, including creating RDS instances, are possible even though the SCP is an allow list.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because an SCP is a policy that grants permissions, the user can perform EC2 and S3 actions even without the administrator policy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All actions are denied, and only the root user of the user's account is unaffected by the SCP and can perform EC2 and S3 actions.

explanation: An SCP does not grant permissions but sets the boundary of the maximum permissions that principals in a member account can have, and the effective permissions are the intersection of the SCP allow and the allow in the user's identity-based policy. Therefore, a user with the administrator policy can perform only the EC2 and S3 actions that the SCP allows, and creating RDS is denied. The administrator policy cannot exceed the SCP. The explanation that an SCP grants permissions directly is wrong, and without a policy there is no allow. The root user of a member account is also affected by SCPs.

prompt: A security team that operates 60 accounts in an organization currently reviews permissions by team every quarter, but cleanup based on usage history is not taking place, so unused roles have accumulated. The team wants to find and clean up IAM roles that have not been used in the last 90 days, as well as service and action permissions that were granted but not used. The team does not want to run scripts in each account and needs to see organization-wide results in one place, and the results must be continuously updated. The delegated administrator account is already designated, and the security team has 4 members. The cleanup targets are thousands of roles, and the results must show the last used service and action information so that the responsible team can check before deletion. Which method is MOST appropriate to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an IAM Access Analyzer for external access with the organization as the zone of trust, and judge unused roles from the results about resources shared with external principals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In the delegated administrator account, create an IAM Access Analyzer for unused access at the organization level, set the tracking period to 90 days, and review the unused findings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Download the IAM credential report from each account every week, merge the last-used date columns, and organize into a table the items that have not been used for more than 90 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Deploy the AWS Config managed rule iam-user-unused-credentials-check as an organization rule to check items with unused credentials.

explanation: An Access Analyzer for unused access can be created at the organization level, continuously updates findings for unused roles, unused credentials, and unused service and action permissions, and lets you specify the unused-access tracking period. An external access analyzer finds access opened to external principals, so it cannot find unused permissions. Credential reports are collected manually per account and cover only user credentials. The Config rule checks only IAM user credentials and does not cover whether roles and permissions are used.

prompt: A company is migrating a MySQL database that it installed and operated directly on EC2 to Amazon RDS for MySQL. The company has only two DBAs, so reducing operational burden is the main reason for the migration, and all settings are subject to audit. The company intends to write a new security checklist after the migration. In the next security audit, the company must provide evidence that distinguishes which controls AWS is responsible for and which controls the company is responsible for. The database contains customer personal information, so both data at rest and data in transit must be protected, and the company wants to write the checklist separating the areas AWS handles from the areas the company handles. Under the shared responsibility model, which TWO responsibilities MOST appropriately remain with the customer after the migration to RDS? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Applying security patches to the host operating system on which the DB instance runs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Designing database user accounts and permissions, and deciding whether to use encryption of data at rest and which KMS key to use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Designing the security groups and subnets that allow access to the DB instance, and setting whether public access is enabled

choices.label: D
choices.text: Managing the security of the hypervisor and physical servers of the hosts on which the DB instance runs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Power and cooling equipment in the data center, and physical destruction of decommissioned storage devices

explanation: The correct answers are the network access configuration and the database account permissions and encryption decisions. Even with a managed service, who can connect through security groups and subnets, the database users and permissions, and whether to use encryption at rest and which key to select are the customer's security responsibilities. The security of the hypervisor and physical servers is security of the cloud itself, which AWS manages. Patching the host operating system is also handled by AWS in RDS, which is different from running it directly on EC2. Data center equipment and the destruction of storage devices are also AWS's physical security responsibilities.

prompt: The HTTPS listener of an ALB for a public web service that general users access with browsers uses 20 ACM public certificates, all issued with email validation. The domains are managed in a single hosted zone in Route 53. A certificate expired because the responsible person missed the renewal confirmation email for one certificate, which caused a service outage. The company wants certificates trusted by public browsers to be maintained and renewed automatically in the future with no human action, with minimal changes. The 20 certificates are for different subdomains and are all attached to ALBs in the same Region. The domain registrar is already in Route 53, so the company has permission to add DNS records directly. Which method is MOST appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Request the certificates again with DNS validation and keep the validation CNAME records in Route 53 so that ACM automatically renews the certificates in use.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Register commercial CA certificates by importing them instead of using ACM, create a scheduled job in each account to re-import the renewed certificate 30 days before expiration, and operate a procedure to manually replace the ALB listener certificate when the renewed certificate is ready.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Issue private certificates from ACM Private CA and attach them to the ALB, and distribute the private root certificate to client devices so that they trust it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive certificate-expiring-soon events through EventBridge and send notifications to the responsible person so that the person does not miss approving the renewal confirmation email.

explanation: An ACM public certificate issued with DNS validation is renewed automatically by ACM as long as the validation CNAME record is maintained, so no human action is needed and browser trust is maintained. Importing commercial CA certificates requires you to automate renewal yourself, which increases the operational burden. Private CA certificates are not trusted by public browsers, which violates the requirements. Expiration notifications leave the manual action of email approval in place, so the same mistake can be repeated.

prompt: A company runs workloads in three Regions, ap-northeast-2, us-east-1, and eu-west-1, and AWS Security Hub CSPM is already enabled in all three Regions. Twelve security analysts work in shifts and want to handle everything in one place without switching consoles. The analysts want to view the findings of all Regions from the console in the single Seoul Region and want the workflow status they change there to be reflected in each original Region as well. The security team has no capacity to operate code directly, and the existing settings in each Region must be kept. All three Regions are in the same AWS account, and Regions may be added in the future. The analysts also want to see insights and control statuses together in the home Region console, and only the security team has permission to modify findings. Which method is MOST appropriate to meet these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Build a pipeline directly that uses Amazon EventBridge rules and AWS Lambda functions to bring each Region's Security Hub CSPM findings back into the Seoul Region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use Security Hub CSPM only in the Seoul Region, and disable the service in the other two Regions to gather the findings in one place.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Export each Region's findings to an Amazon S3 bucket, build a dashboard that combines them with Amazon Athena queries, and have analysts manage status there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Designate the Seoul Region as the home Region, turn on cross-Region aggregation, and select us-east-1 and eu-west-1 as linked Regions.

explanation: With cross-Region aggregation, once you set the home Region and choose linked Regions, findings, insights, and control statuses are replicated to the home Region, and updates made in the home Region are also replicated back to the linked Regions. An EventBridge and Lambda pipeline requires operating code you build yourself and requires separate implementation of reverse reflection of status, which violates the requirements. Enabling only the home Region means findings for resources in the other Regions are not generated at all, so visibility is lost. The combination of S3 and Athena is read-only analysis and cannot reflect workflow status in the original findings.

prompt: In an organization that uses 180 accounts and 4 Regions, the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices (FSBP) standard in AWS Security Hub must be enabled in all accounts and Regions, and member account administrators must not be able to turn it off arbitrarily. New accounts must also automatically receive the same settings. The standard enablement status is checked in regular audits, and a situation in which settings differ between accounts is considered a security incident. Some existing accounts have already turned on Security Hub with local settings. The security team wants to make configuration changes only from a single delegated administrator account. Once central configuration is applied, account administrators must be prevented from turning off the standard directly in the console, and the audit team wants to see on a single screen which policy is applied to which account. Which method prevents configuration drift with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the delegated administrator account, turn on central configuration, and attach a configuration policy with FSBP enabled to the organization root to designate the accounts as centrally managed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use AWS CloudFormation StackSets to deploy a stack that enables the FSBP standard to all accounts and Regions, and add stack instances for new accounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Have each member account administrator turn on the standard directly, check whether the standard is disabled with an AWS Config rule, and send a notification to accounts that violate it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keep local configuration, and specify in the delegated administrator account's settings that Security Hub and the default standards be turned on automatically for new organization accounts.

explanation: The correct answer is a central configuration configuration policy. The delegated administrator applies Security Hub, the FSBP standard, and the controls in one step to the home Region and linked Regions with a configuration policy. For centrally managed accounts, only the delegated administrator can change the settings, so drift is prevented, and attaching it to the root makes new accounts inherit it. Auto-enable under local configuration applies only to new accounts and the current Region, so drift arises in existing accounts or other Regions. StackSets cannot prevent member administrators from turning off the standard in the console. Manual enablement with after-the-fact checks requires human involvement and is not preventive.
